extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, students of aesthetics, and creative writers interested in theory of the sublime, beauty, and simplicity
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing aesthetic value in poetry and art focused on the distinctions among the agreeable, the good, the beautiful, and the sublime, and on conditions for 'simple' or 'sentimental' poetry. Includes how scale, terror, nature, and sincerity affect aesthetic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four aesthetic categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes of aesthetic value: the agreeable, the good, the sublime, and the beautiful; 'the sublime and the beautiful only belong properly to art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy as the primary classification when evaluating art: identify which of the four categories a work primarily appeals to and whether it aspires to art's end (pleasure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreeable (sensory pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreeable only pleases the senses; 'it only pleases by its matter ... The agreeable only pleases by its matter, for it is only matter that can affect the senses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether pleasure derives solely from immediate sensory states (ephemeral, subject-dependent). The agreeable 'is agreeable only inasmuch as it is felt by the subject' and lacks objective foundation; it changes with the subject's state (e.g., warmth vs. coolness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good (rational pleasure / moral/ intellectual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The good 'pleases reason' and 'is perceived by thought'; it is that 'in which reason recognizes a conformity with her theoretical and practical laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work accords with principles intelligible to reason (ethical, logical, theoretical). The good provides objective foundation and 'widens our understanding'; its pleasure is tied to concept and esteem rather than sense-based inclination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful (form-mediated sensuous and rational pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful 'pleases through the medium of the senses ... but it pleases reason, on account of its form'; it 'only pleases the reasonable subject in so far as it is also a sensuous subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether aesthetic pleasure arises from formal properties (shape, proportion, harmony) that can be intuited sensuously yet claim universal assent—beauty is not merely subjective sensation but involves form that resonates with reason and remains 'independent of all empirical limitations of sensuousness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish which faculty is pleased
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a response to an object is: agreeable (senses), beautiful (intuition/form pleasing reason), or good (conception/pleasing to reason). 'The good is perceived by thought, the beautiful by intuition, and the agreeable only by the senses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing a piece, explicitly identify which faculty the work addresses and whether that is appropriate to the work's aims; this helps explain transient appeal (agreeable) versus objective worth (good/beautiful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime (opposition to sensuousness and excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an object to be called sublime it 'must be in opposition with our sensuousness.' Two kinds are given: 'the sublime of knowledge and the sublime of force.' The sublime arises when an object 'exceeds in its quantity the capacity of our imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge sublimity by whether an object overwhelms imagination (scale, magnitude, or force) without fully paralyzing faculties, provoking an elevation of mind. Distinguish whether the source is cognitive (ideas exceeding representation) or dynamic/forceful (threatening power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime requires self-conscious elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: The observer's consciousness must find support in a 'higher consciousness of its independent strength and dignity.' 'This consciousness of ourselves must always dominate in order that the great and the horrible may have for us an aesthetic value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work enables the reader/viewer to feel elevated rather than overwhelmed; the aesthetic value of the great/terrible depends on maintaining self-conscious dignity rather than being reduced to helplessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime (quantity/scale as a test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is reduced to impotence when an object 'exceeds in its quantity the capacity of our imagination' (e.g., a mountain enlarged beyond comprehension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scale and complexity as indicators: very large, multitudinous, or conceptually vast elements can generate the sublime when they push pictorial imagination to its limits and thus call forth reflective ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terror/horror can produce aesthetic pleasure if not paralytic
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects 'ugly, revolting, and horrifying to the senses' can still 'please' and even yield a feeling 'which we cannot properly call a pleasure, but one which we often like much more than pleasure.' Examples: storms, the Furies, Medea, Clytemnestra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating depictions of horror/terror, check that they inspire an interest and elevation (the awful mixed with reflection) rather than mere disgust or paralytic fear; the tragic/terrible must engage higher mental faculties for aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of threat and mitigation affects pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding elements that increase threat (leaning mountain) can increase aesthetic interest via terror; measures that reduce perceived threat (prop up the mountain, terraces) diminish that pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how compositional choices (introducing scale, isolation, threat) influence the balance between terror and pleasure; deliberate mitigation will lower sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The great and the terrible as sources of pleasure only with reflective distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The great and terrible 'throw our souls into an anxious agitation' while the mind 'falls back on itself by reflection' and finds dignity; this reflective distance is necessary for aesthetic enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work provides enough contemplative distance (narrative framing, aesthetic mediation) so that awe/terror translates into reflective elevation rather than mere panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-inspired feeling requires genuineness and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Two necessary conditions for nature to inspire 'a sort of love and respectful emotion': (1) 'the object ... must be really nature, or something we take for nature'; (2) 'this object must be in the full sense of the word simple.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or judging 'sentimental' or 'simple' poetry, ensure depictions feel genuinely natural (not artful imitation) and present nature in a way that contrasts clearly with artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature's appeal is moral (conception), not merely aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling excited by nature 'is not a satisfaction of the aesthetical taste, but a satisfaction of the moral sense; for it is produced by means of a conception and not immediately by the single fact of intuition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish sentimental responses grounded in ideas (memory, moral symbolism, nostalgia) from responses based purely on formal beauty; judge sentimental poetry for depth of idea rather than merely picturesque description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity must be an internal necessity, not insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature must triumph 'not by its blind and brutal force as a dynamical power, but in virtue of its form as a moral magnitude; in a word, not as a want, but as an internal necessity.' 'Insufficiency is only a want and a defect, and nothing that results from a want or defect could produce esteem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether apparent simplicity is a moral/formal choice (worthy) rather than mere incompetence or lack; true simplicity should express necessity and integrity rather than deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish simplicity as surprise vs. simplicity of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity as surprise: involuntary, causes 'gayety' and raillery but mixed with esteem for truth; simplicity of feeling: conscious merit, inspires deeper admiration. 'Simplicity as a surprise ... in the former case it is simplicity as a surprise, and the impression resulting from it is one of gayety; in the second case, it is simplicity of feeling, and we are moved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing character or voice, identify whether simplicity is accidental (comic/naïve) or deliberate (noble/virtuous); responses and critical stance should differ accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity/natural truth commands esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Even involuntary simplicity 'puts the person to the blush' yet 'we experience ... a really moral pleasure' because 'we must esteem truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value authenticity and truthfulness in expression; even when simplicity is comic, it can command moral esteem if it reveals unfeigned truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Childlike (noble) vs childish (foolish) simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Childlike simplicity is 'a superior force (practically), a heart-full of truth and innocence' and provokes esteem; childish simplicity exposes 'a weak side' and provokes raillery. 'Nor is it always such an easy matter to distinguish exactly childish candor from childlike candor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully judge whether a 'simple' voice or persona is meant to be experienced as innocent and morally upright (childlike) or merely naive/foolish (childish); context and indications of moral insight determine the reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity depends on moral disposition; beware of affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: This interest in nature 'can only manifest itself in a soul capable of ideas, that is, in a moral soul.' 'For the immense majority it is nothing more than pure affectation ... this taste of sentimentality ... by no means proves that true refinement of sense has become general.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising sentimental or pastoral poetic styles, distinguish genuine moral-sentimental feeling from fashionable affectation; authenticity requires a moral/intellectual capacity, not merely surface gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual suitability of simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity may be admirable in private life but imprudent or damaging in certain public or political roles (example: Pope Adrian VI's candid avowals were 'supremely imprudent' though they might merit esteem if they were genuine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a simple (sincere) stance suits the social function or role of the speaker/character; virtues in one context can be strategic faults in another—criticize accordingly.
